17.0.0.en: 1 The burden of Damascus. Behold, Damascus is taken away from being a city, and it shall be a ruinous heap. 2 The cities of Aroer are forsaken: they shall be for flocks, which shall lie down, and none shall make them afraid.

17.0.1.en: Damascus is considered one of the most ancient cities; it is mentioned in the days of Abraham (Gen 14:15); King David conquered it and set a garrison in it (2 Sam 8:5-6; 1 Chr 18:5-6). Rezon arose and was able to found the Syrian kingdom, and war between it and Israel lasted a long time, but later they allied together against Judah and Assyria. It suffered defeat several times: in 843 BC Shalmaneser attacked Damascus and defeated its king Hazael, and Tiglath-pileser attacked it in 732 BC, killed its king Rezin and led its people into captivity (2 Kgs 16:5-9; Isa 7:1-8; Amos 1:3-5). Afterward it passed from the Assyrians to the Chaldeans, then to the Persians, then to the Macedonian Greeks, then to the Romans at the hands of Metellus in 64 BC, and Syria became a Roman province in 63 BC.

17.0.2.en: If Damascus allied itself with Ephraim against Judah, the punishment fell upon Damascus and Ephraim together. They represent the evil powers of the world that resist the truth, as it is written in the Book of Revelation: “And the fourth angel poured out his vial upon the sun; and power was given unto him to scorch men with fire. And men were scorched with great heat, and blasphemed the name of God, which hath power over these plagues: and they repented not to give him glory” (Rev 16:19).

17.0.3.en: “Behold, Damascus is taken away from being a city, and it shall be a ruinous heap. The cities of Aroer are forsaken: they shall be for flocks, which shall lie down, and none shall make them afraid” [1-2].

17.0.4.en: Damascus was very prosperous until Tiglath-pileser the Assyrian besieged it, killed its king and took its people captive, and it became like a ruinous heap.

17.0.5.en: As for Aroer, there are at least 3 cities bearing the same name [Aroer is a Moabite name meaning “naked” or “nakedness”]: a city in Moab, now called Ara'ir, about twelve miles east of the Dead Sea, a little south of Dhiban and north of the river Arnon; a village in the southern part of Judea (1 Sam 30:28), now called Ar'arah, twelve miles southeast of Beersheba; and the third, which is the one meant here, a city in Gilead near Rabbah, which is Rabbah of Ammon (Josh 13:25; Judg 11:33), Amman, the capital of Jordan.

17.0.6.en: Damascus and Aroer represent the soul that exalts itself against God and allies itself with others against His Church; even though God leaves it for a time to appear strong, successful and prosperous, it returns and collapses in two ways:

17.0.7.en: a. It is turned from a great city into a ruinous heap, that is, it loses its life, because it withdraws from God Himself, the source of life.

17.0.8.en: b. Like Aroer it is turned from a dwelling for people (with God) into a pasture for flocks and animals, as though our resistance to the truth causes us to lose our dignity and turns our life into a playground for every beast, so that we bear the animal, carnal nature. Therefore St. Ephrem the Syrian praises the Child of the manger, saying: [Glory to Him who looked upon us, how we had consented to resemble the beasts in our frenzy and greed, and came down to us and became one of us, that we might become heavenly].

17.1.0.en: 3 The fortress also shall cease from Ephraim, and the kingdom from Damascus, and the remnant of Syria: they shall be as the glory of the children of Israel, saith the LORD of hosts. 4 And in that day it shall come to pass, that the glory of Jacob shall be humbled, and the fatness of his flesh shall wax lean. 5 And it shall be as when the harvestman gathereth the corn, and reapeth the ears with his arm; and it shall be as he that gathereth ears in the valley of Rephaim. 6 Yet gleaning shall be left in it, as the shaking of an olive tree, two or three berries in the top of the uppermost bough, four or five in the outmost fruitful branches thereof, saith the LORD God of Israel. 7 At that day shall a man look to his Maker, and his eyes shall have respect to the Holy One of Israel. 8 And he shall not look to the altars, the work of his hands, neither shall respect that which his fingers have made, the poles and the sun-images. 9 In that day shall his strong cities be as a ruin in the forest, and the high places which they left because of the children of Israel: and there shall be desolation. 10 Because thou hast forgotten the God of thy salvation, and hast not been mindful of the rock of thy strength, therefore shalt thou plant pleasant plants, and shalt set it with strange slips: 11 In the day of thy planting thou shalt hedge it in, and in the morning shalt thou make thy seed to flourish: but the harvest shall flee away in the day of the deadly stroke and of hopeless sorrow.

17.1.1.en: Damascus took the lead in the idea of an alliance against Judah, therefore it deserved to be punished first; and when Israel grew weak and submitted to the counsel, it too deserved harsh discipline, though the door of hope was opened before it and the existence of a faithful and sincere remnant enjoying God's salvation was announced.

17.1.2.en: The prophecy presents the natural fruit of the evil alliance, in which there is reliance on the human arm and purely human thought while ignoring the divine work; this fruit is a natural punishment under which man falls in his evil:

17.1.3.en: a. Loss of fortification: “The fortress also shall cease from Ephraim” [3]; “In that day shall his strong cities be as a ruin in the forest, and the high places which they left because of the children of Israel: and there shall be desolation” [9].

17.2.0.en: If God, the God of our salvation, is the rock of our fortress [10], then our withdrawing from Him and our rejection of His work is the passing away of the true fortress... Then fortresses cannot protect our inner city, but become like a ruin in the midst of the forest, of no value, and like abandoned high places which have the outward appearance without the power of action!

17.2.1.en: God is our fortress in which we take refuge, and our depths find rest; then all the powers of darkness cannot creep in upon us.

17.2.2.en: b. Loss of inward glory: “And in that day it shall come to pass, that the glory of Jacob shall be humbled” [4]. If the king's daughter is all glorious within (Ps 45), then the secret of her glory is her Christ who dwells in her, who establishes His Kingdom within her. In Christ Jesus we are glorified not only before men but also before the Father, as St. Jerome says: [Look upon us, and you will see your Son dwelling in us].

17.2.3.en: c. Loss of strength: “and the fatness of his flesh shall wax lean” [4]; therefore the Lord Christ says: “Without me ye can do nothing” (Jn 15:5).

17.2.4.en: * We cannot run in the way of God unless we are carried on the wings of the Spirit.

17.2.5.en: * No one is stronger than he who enjoys heavenly help, and no one is weaker than he who is deprived of it.

17.2.6.en: * We fear nothing, for in order to overcome Satan we must know that our skill will profit nothing, and that everything is of God's grace.

17.2.7.en: St. John Chrysostom. d. Loss of fruit: the valley of Rephaim was known for the fertility of its land and the abundance of its fruits and crops, but because of the enemies nothing is left to Ephraim but to gather the ears that fall behind the harvesters and to collect what remains at the top of the olive branches, only two or three berries [5-6], that is, they become like the poor who have nothing to harvest (Deut 24:20).

17.3.0.en: They hedge in the fields and sow, but at the time of harvest the enemy comes to seize it, leaving them what falls from him on the ground, and the feasts of harvest turn into times of gloom and hopelessness [11]. In other words, they lose the fruit of their labor and forfeit their joy and peace.

17.3.1.en: Now we ask: why does God permit Ephraim this humiliation?

17.3.2.en: That he may return to God his Creator, instead of sharing with the Arameans their evil counsels, their idolatrous worship and their unclean abominations, for it says: “At that day shall a man look to his Maker, and his eyes shall have respect to the Holy One of Israel. And he shall not look to the altars, the work of his hands, neither shall respect that which his fingers have made, the poles Asherahs and the sun-images hammanum” [7-8].

17.3.3.en: The poles here mean the statues and images of the goddess of love and beauty (Ishtar), corresponding to Aphrodite, which were set on poles (like pillars of wood). This goddess is counted the wife and companion of the god Baal, so his altar is surrounded by a group of trees or poles bearing statues of the goddess, as a sign of her fertility.

17.3.4.en: These poles and trees carried licentious sexual meanings, so worship was mixed with uncleanness as an inseparable part of it (Ex 34:13; Deut 16:21; Judg 6:25; 2 Chr 34:4-7; Mic 5:14). God permitted the discipline of His people so that they might not defile their view of sex, but lift their heart and mind toward God, who is above sex and who grants us holiness in married life and in bodily relations.

17.3.5.en: As for the sun-images, some have translated the Hebrew word as sun-gods, and some have translated it Baal-hamman, the Syrian sun god, while others have translated it “altar of incense,” on which incense was offered to the sun god; so this expression is particular to pagan worship, distinct from the holy incense that is offered in the temple.

17.4.0.en: 12 Ah! the noise of many peoples, which make a noise like the noise of the seas; and the rushing of tribes, that make a rushing like the rushing of mighty waters! 13 The tribes shall rush like the rushing of many waters: but he shall rebuke them, and they shall flee far off, and shall be chased as the chaff of the mountains before the wind, and like a rolling thing before the whirlwind. 14 And behold at eveningtide terror; and before the morning they are not. This is the portion of them that spoil us, and the lot of them that rob us.

17.4.1.en: He likens the enemies to the sea that cannot be resisted... God permitted the many peoples to descend upon Ephraim like many waters to drown it, and yet God has set a limit for the sea. He permits it to drown up to a certain point and for a time, while He keeps the faithful few of His children safe from the sea's raging and tumult.

17.4.2.en: In a wonderful portrayal he says: “Ah! the noise of many peoples... the tribes shall rush like the rushing of many waters: but he shall rebuke them, and they shall flee far off, and shall be chased as the chaff of the mountains before the wind, and like a rolling thing before the whirlwind. And behold at eveningtide terror; and before the morning they are not. This is the portion of them that spoil us, and the lot of them that rob us” [12-14].

17.4.3.en: God permits the enemies to attack like the waters of mighty seas before which no one can stand, but when He rebukes them they become like chaff in the blast of the wind upon the mountains, with no place to settle and no power to resist, or like a wheel rolling before a whirlwind that cannot be stopped. Our enemy is exceedingly violent: when we leave ourselves in his hands he draws us into his whirlpool to drown us in the depths of his sea; but when we are hidden in the Lord the enemy becomes as nothing before us, withdrawing like chaff before the fiery wind of the Holy Spirit and rolling away before the active word of God.

17.5.0.en: Therefore he says: “at eveningtide terror” [14], meaning that when the Sun of righteousness is absent from our life, darkness comes upon us and we become as in the evening, so that the enemy finds a place in us and terrifies us; but before the morning, that is, at dawn, when our Christ shines in us, the enemy becomes as nothing and is counted as non-existent. This is his portion: he had plundered our life and robbed us of our glory, but he returns and is shattered before Him who dwells in us.

18.0.0.en: 1 O land of the rustling of wings, which is beyond the rivers of Cush: 2 That sendeth ambassadors by the sea, even in vessels of bulrushes upon the waters, saying, Go, ye swift messengers, to a nation tall and bare, to a people terrible from their beginning hitherto; a nation of power and strength and treading down, whose land the rivers have cut through! 3 All ye inhabitants of the world, and dwellers on the earth, see ye, when he lifteth up an ensign on the mountains; and when he bloweth a trumpet, hear ye. 4 For so the LORD said unto me, I will be still, and I will consider in my dwelling place like a clear heat upon herbs, and like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest. 5 For afore the harvest, when the bud is perfect, and the flower becometh a ripe grape, he shall cut off the shoots with sickles, and take away and cast down the branches. 6 They shall be left together unto the fowls of the mountains, and to the beasts of the earth: and the fowls shall summer upon them, and all the beasts of the earth shall winter upon them.

18.0.1.en: The prophet directs his speech to Cush, saying: “O land of the rustling of wings, which is beyond the rivers of Cush” [1].

18.0.2.en: What is meant by the land of the rustling of wings?

18.0.3.en: a. Some see that it is a reference to the imperial power that spread its wings over all the land of Cush and its surroundings. The Holy Bible has used this figure many times; it is said of the king of Assyria, “and the stretching out of his wings shall fill the breadth of thy land, O Immanuel” (Isa 8:8). The king of Assyria is also likened to a great eagle with great wings (Ezek 17).

18.0.4.en: b. Some scholars see that the rustling of wings points to the power and greatness of Egypt, while others see that it is Great Britain, which bore great glories across the seas, and others counted it the United States of America, which takes the eagle as its emblem.

18.0.5.en: c. The rustling of wings points to insects, so it is a symbol of Cush as a country famous for its flying insects; especially since the Hebrew word here, silsal, was used in Deut 28:42 of insects (crickets).

18.0.6.en: d. The word sel means “shadow,” so it points to a country near the equator, where the shadow is doubled (or is significant because of the intensity of the heat).

18.0.7.en: e. Some based their interpretation on what is found in the Septuagint and the Targum, that the rustling of wings points to ships; as though the prophet were saying that the ships of Ethiopia sail with their sails spread like the wings of insects. Sailors used to call the sail a wing.

18.0.8.en: In any case the king of Ethiopia sent messengers by his ships made of papyrus, and he was in haste, because the enemy was at the gates and represented a danger to the whole world at that time. The Ethiopians were known for their ability to spy on the positions and movements of enemies by means of their small, swift ships, so the king did not hesitate to move in order to call Judah to an alliance against the growing danger of Assyria.

18.1.0.en: The king's mission was for an alliance, but it was not a mission of peace; rather it was a mission calling to war against Assyria and revolt against Sennacherib, a matter that all the peoples were awaiting, for it was said: “All ye inhabitants of the world, and dwellers on the earth, see ye, when he lifteth up an ensign (the banner of war) on the mountains; and when he bloweth a trumpet, hear ye” [3].

18.1.1.en: Would that the messengers of the Gospel bore the same zeal as the king of Ethiopia and his messengers, who were called to set out so that all might ally together, not against Assyria but against the enemy of good, when the banner of the Cross is lifted up and the trumpet of the word of God is blown, and the spiritual battle is joined under the leadership of the incarnate, crucified divine Word, who carries us in Himself and hides us in His pierced side, granting us the spirit of conquest and victory. He entered the battle through His temptation on the mountain and was victorious in our name and on our behalf, and He continued to strive for us until He completed His striving by the Cross.

18.1.2.en: * The Lord gave us by His example how we can be victorious, when He was tempted.

18.1.3.en: Abba Serapion * Jesus our Leader permitted Himself to be tempted in order to teach His children how to fight.

18.1.4.en: St. Augustine. The prophet says: “Go, ye swift messengers, to a nation tall and bare, to a people terrible from their beginning hitherto; a nation of power and strength and treading down, whose land the rivers have cut through” [2].

18.1.5.en: Some see that the description there applies to the Ethiopians or the Assyrians or the Medes... but the mission was directed to the people of God, who were called “a people terrible,” because their God is a terrible God (Ex 23:27; 34:10; Deut 28:58; Josh 2:9; Ps 139:14). They are a people terrible from their beginning, that is, from the start of their formation, as they came out of Egypt with a mighty hand and a high arm. As for his saying, “whose land the rivers have cut through” [2], it points to the gravity of its position, because the enemy is about to attack it, and he will be like a sweeping river; and its description as “a nation tall (stretched out) and bare (sharp)” [2] is, in the Septuagint, “a nation crushed and torn”... as the enemy draws the people like sheep and they drag them into captivity, so that they are dragged away.

18.1.6.en: If the prophet asks the people not to accept the mission of the king of Cush to ally together, what then is God's position concerning the attacks of Assyria upon His people?

18.2.0.en: “For so the LORD said unto me, I will be still, and I will consider in my dwelling place like a clear heat upon herbs, and like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest” [4]. It seems as though God is calm and still, not concerned with our affairs, and God may leave the tyrannical king of Assyria to destroy and ruin and shatter cities until he reaches the gates of Jerusalem; then God declares His hidden role and turns the king of Assyria back disappointed, his pride and his army shattered.

18.2.1.en: God, the Governor of all, cares for every small and great matter, but in His longsuffering we think that He has forgotten us or does not care about our condition, so we say with the psalmist: “Do not forsake us utterly (greatly),” for even in what seems as though He has left us, He is ordering the matter for our salvation and edification.

18.2.2.en: St. John Chrysostom likens God to a nurse who places her hands in the hands of the little child to train him to walk; and suddenly she withdraws her hands from him and he falls, and lifts his eyes to her, reproaching her with his tears, but she returns and holds his hands... In this way he is trained to walk. She leaves him by the hands, but she will not leave him in her thought or her heart.

18.2.3.en: What we call forsaking is care, for God looks upon us in our affliction and turns the bitter into a heat that gives ripeness to the herbs, or like a cloud in the heat of harvest that gives moisture and shade... outwardly sufferings, inwardly edification and rest!

18.3.0.en: He also sees in afflictions a kind of “pruning of trees,” that is, removing the superfluous branches so that the tree may bring forth abundant fruit [5].

18.4.0.en: Finally, after He permitted Sennacherib to be victorious over many cities of Judah, He shattered him and his army before he entered Jerusalem, so that their corpses became food for the beasts and the birds of prey [6], for 185 thousand of the army of Sennacherib died in one day.

18.5.s.en: 2. Cush offers a gift to God:

18.5.0.en: 7 In that day shall a present be brought unto the LORD of hosts of a people tall and bare, and from a people terrible from their beginning hitherto; a nation of power and strength and treading down, whose land the rivers have cut through, to the place of the name of the LORD of hosts, the mount Zion.

18.5.1.en: If Cush or Egypt or other nations think that they are able to protect the people of God from Assyria, all the nations will discover that they need the One who came out of the tribe of Judah to protect them from the devil and all his evil works; then the nations that were stricken with arrogance will come in submission to bring a gift to the LORD of hosts [7] in mount Zion, that is, in His Church.

18.5.2.en: The prophet Isaiah saw countless numbers of kings, rulers and great men coming to Jerusalem to worship the true King, who bore on His head not a temporal crown but a crown of thorns. He saw the believers as spiritual kings submitting to the King of kings, the Lord of glory Jesus, who came out of the tribe of Judah.
